Enhanced-Entropy Phases in Geometrically Frustrated Pyrochlore Magnets

Prakash Timsina Affiliation: Department of Physics, New Mexico State University, Las Cruces, NM 88001, USA    Andres Chappa Affiliation: Department of Physics, New Mexico State University, Las Cruces, NM 88001, USA    Deema Alyones Affiliation: Department of Chemical and Materials Engineering, New Mexico State University, Las Cruces, NM 88001, USA Affiliation: Department of Physics, New Mexico State University, Las Cruces, NM 88001, USA    Igor Vasiliev Affiliation: Department of Physics, New Mexico State University, Las Cruces, NM 88001, USA    Ludi Miao* Affiliation: Department of Physics, New Mexico State University, Las Cruces, NM 88001, USA
August 24, 2026
Abstract

∗ Email: lmiao@nmsu.edu

Frustrated magnets provide a platform for exploring exotic phases beyond conventional ordering, with potential relevance to functional materials and information technologies. In this work, we use Monte Carlo simulations to map the thermodynamic phase diagram of pyrochlore iridates R2R_{2}Ir2O7 (RR = Dy, Ho) with three stable magnetic ground-state phases: frustrated spin-ice 2-in–2-out (2I2O) phase, frustrated fragmented 3-in–1-out/1-in–3-out (3I1O/1I3O) phase, and antiferromagnetic all-in–all-out (AIAO) phase without frustration. We investigate the physical origin of two enhanced-entropy (EE) phases at finite temperatures, which emerge at the boundaries between stable phases. These EE phases exhibit high magnetic susceptibility and high entropy without long-range order. Their stabilization arises from entropic minimization of the free energy, where the entropy dominates energetic competition near phase boundaries at finite temperatures. Our results demonstrate a platform to engineer highly susceptible and degenerated states through frustration and thermal activation, offering a foundation for the design of entropy-based materials and phases in correlated systems.

Introduction

Entropy, which arises from extensive configurational degeneracy, is pivotal in stabilizing exotic phases and emergent functionalities, spanning from chemically disordered high-entropy alloys [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 8] and entropy-stabilized ceramics [10, 11] to geometrically frustrated states such as quantum spin liquids [12, 13, 14, 15], spin ice [16, 17, 18], and frustrated pyrochlore magnets [19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25]. Among these examples, pyrochlore magnets stand out for highly tunable magnetic structures and degrees of frustration, arising from a delicate balance of competing interactions [26]. In these systems, entropically rich phases transcend conventional magnetic order and serve as a platform for realizing two-dimensional magnetic monopole gases (2DMG) [27, 28], which carry a non-zero net magnetic charge. To date, most investigations have focused on ground-state properties, leaving the thermodynamic behavior of frustrated phases at finite temperatures largely unexplored. Recently, Lu et al. [30] reported strain-induced enhanced-entropy (EE) states in pyrochlore spin ice at low temperatures; however, the origin and how to engineer such EE states remain poorly understood.

In this study, we explore frustrated pyrochlore magnets R2R_{2}Ir2O7 (RR = Dy, Ho) by tuning the dd-ff exchange interactions between R3+R^{3+} moments and neighboring Ir4+\text{Ir}^{4+} moments. Here, we systematically investigate the thermodynamic behavior and physical origin of two EE phases located at boundaries between three well-known stable phases: “2 spins in–2 spins out” (2I2O) spin ice phase, “3 spins in–1 spin out/1 spin in–3 spins out” (3I1O/1I3O) fragmented phase, and “all spins in–all spins out” (AIAO) antiferromagnetic state [26]. These EE phases are characterized by high entropy and high magnetic susceptibility, which are established only at finite temperatures. Our results indicate that these EE phases emerge through entropic stabilization due to free energy minimization, exhibiting distinct thermodynamic signatures from spin ice phase, fragmented phase, and antiferromagnetic phase, thus identifying a new class of EE magnetic states. Our findings reveal a foundation for engineering EE states in correlated magnetic systems, enabling the design of advanced materials with tunable memory and topological properties.

Results and discussions

A. Tunable Magnetic Ground States and Frustration Levels

In pyrochlore iridates R2R_{2}Ir2O7 (R=R= Ho, Dy), both R3+R^{3+} and Ir4+ ions form interconnected networks of corner-sharing tetrahedra, as illustrated in Fig. 1. The Ir4+ sublattice forms AIAO antiferromagnetic order below TN∼130T_{N}\sim 130 K, while the R3+R^{3+} moments typically order into a 2I2O spin ice configuration at T∼1T\sim 1 K. The disparity in these ordering temperatures results in the Ir4+ moments acting as a static antiferromagnetic background field HlocH_{\text{loc}} on the R3+R^{3+} sublattice via dd–ff exchange coupling. The large (∼10​μB\sim 10\mu_{\text{B}}) R3+R^{3+} moments are strongly constrained by crystal-field and spin–orbit interactions to align along the local ⟨111⟩\langle 111\rangle axes, making a classical two-state Ising description an appropriate framework [29, 26]. To quantitatively investigate the magnetic frustrations in pyrochlore iridates, we follow the classical nearest-neighbor pseudo-Ising Hamiltonian established for R2R_{2}Ir2O7 (R=R= Ho, Dy) [26] and systematically vary HlocH_{\text{loc}}:

ℋ=Jeff​∑⟨i,j⟩σi​σj−16​Hloc​∑⟨i,α⟩σi​σα,\mathscr{H}=J_{\text{eff}}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\sigma_{i}\sigma_{j}-\frac{1}{6}H_{\text{loc}}\sum_{\langle i,\alpha\rangle}\sigma_{i}\sigma_{\alpha}, (1)

where σi=±1\sigma_{i}=\pm 1 represents the pseudo-Ising spins of R3+R^{3+} ions, and σα\sigma_{\alpha} denotes the frozen AIAO-ordered spins of the Ir4+ sublattice which is treated as a static background. The first term denotes the nearest-neighbor interactions among the R3+R^{3+} spins, while the second term indicates the interactions between R3+R^{3+} spins σi\sigma_{i} and the static Ir4+\mathrm{Ir}^{4+} background spins σα\sigma_{\alpha}. We perform Monte Carlo simulations using the Metropolis algorithm [26, 27, 28] by evolving the R3+R^{3+} spin configurations, with the Ir4+ sublattice held fixed throughout.

We calculate the magnetic order parameter MM defined by:

M=|1N​∑i=1NΔi​qi|,M=\left|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Delta_{i}q_{i}\right|, (2)

where Δi=+1\Delta_{i}=+1 (−1-1) for inward (outward) tetrahedra and qiq_{i} is the magnetic charge index (all-in is 2, 3I1O is 1, 2I2O is 0, and so on) as a function of kB​T/Jeffk_{\text{B}}T/J_{\text{eff}} and Hloc/JeffH_{\text{loc}}/J_{\text{eff}}. The result demonstrates three distinct magnetic ground state phases consistent with previous studies [26]: the highly degenerate phase with 2I2O spin structure (phase I) for Hloc/Jeff<2H_{\text{loc}}/J_{\text{eff}}<2, the fragmented phase with 3I1O/1I3O spin structure (phase II) for 2<Hloc/Jeff<62<H_{\text{loc}}/J_{\text{eff}}<6, and the antiferromagnetic phase with AIAO spin structure (phase III) for Hloc/Jeff>6H_{\text{loc}}/J_{\text{eff}}>6 as shown in Fig. 1. We also compute the normalized entropy per rare-earth moment S⁡(T)/S∞S(T)/S_{\infty} as a map of kB​T/Jeffk_{\text{B}}T/J_{\text{eff}} and Hloc/JeffH_{\text{loc}}/J_{\text{eff}}, where

S⁡(T)=S∞−∫T∞Cv​(T′)T′​d​T′S(T)=S_{\infty}-\int_{T}^{\infty}\frac{C_{v}(T^{\prime})}{T^{\prime}}dT^{\prime} (3)

and S∞=kB​ln⁡(2)S_{\infty}=k_{\text{B}}\ln(2) is the infinite temperature entropy, as shown in Fig. 1. As expected, these phases exhibit distinct entropy behaviors that reflect their underlying frustration levels: the 2I2O phase retains significant nonzero spin ice Pauling entropy of S=12​kB​ln⁡(1.5)S=\frac{1}{2}k_{\text{B}}\ln(1.5) per spin [16], the 3I1O/1I3O phase carries intermediate entropy of S≈12​kB​ln⁡(1.3)S\approx\frac{1}{2}k_{\text{B}}\ln(1.3) per spin [31], and the unfrustrated AIAO phase with zero entropy.

B. Thermodynamic Signatures Across Phase Boundaries

To understand the thermodynamic behavior across different magnetic phases, we analyze the temperature dependence of magnetic susceptibility χ\chi and specific heat capacity CvC_{v}. In the stable phases, i.e. 2I2O (phase I), 3I1O/1I3O (phase II), and AIAO (phase III), each phase exhibits a broad, thermally activated peak in both χ\chi and CvC_{v} in transition temperature regions, which are labeled with shaded regions as shown in Fig. 2. The approximate alignment of CvC_{v} and χ\chi peaks indicate that spin ordering and thermal energy fluctuations occur cooperatively in the approach to magnetic orders.

However, this behavior changes significantly near the phase boundaries that separate these stable phases. In the vicinity of the phase boundary (PB) I–II, the temperature dependent behaviors in χ\chi and CvC_{v} begin to decouple. For example, at PB I–II [Fig. 2], CvC_{v} exhibits a peak at around kB​T/Jeffk_{\text{B}}T/J_{\text{eff}} = 2.13 (TT = 3 K), indicating a phase transition, whereas χ\chi increases monotonically without a peak toward the ground state. At vicinities of PB I-II on both sides, CvC_{v} exhibits two peaks indicating two phase transitions with a EE phase at finite temperature, whereas χ\chi only exhibits one peak. Similar behavior is observed around PB II-III as shown in Fig. 2. We have varied the system sizes to confirm that the reported results are independent of finite-size effects (see Note 1 of Supplemental Material) [32]. These behaviors are atypical for stable ground states and can be attributed to free spins mimicking thermal fluctuations, as detailed in Note 2 of Supplemental Material [32]. The appearance of such anomalies further motivates a broader exploration of the temperature–field phase space, as discussed below.

C. Demonstration of EE Phases

To explore the thermodynamic landscape beyond the stable phases at the ground state, we map the magnetic susceptibility χ\chi and specific heat CvC_{\text{v}} over a broad range of kB​T/Jeffk_{\text{B}}T/J_{\text{eff}} and local static field Hloc/JeffH_{\text{loc}}/J_{\text{eff}}. The specific heat CvC_{\text{v}} exhibits one peak near the center of the stable phases, i.e.Hloc/Jeff=2,4,8H_{\text{loc}}/J_{\text{eff}}=2,4,8, whereas around the phase boundaries it bifurcates and exhibits two peaks. Between those peaks, CvC_{\text{v}} has a small value close to 0, indicating the existence of new phases, as shown in Fig. 3. Since they exist at finite temperatures and at the vicinity of phase boundaries, we tentatively name them EEI-II\text{EE}_{\text{I-II}} and EEII-III\text{EE}_{\text{II-III}}, where “EE” stands for EE phases. These phases are consistent with previously reported step-like behavior in the magentic order parameter at finite temperature in the same system [26]. The presence of such EE states is further supported by the behavior of the magnetic susceptibility χ\chi, which remains significantly elevated across these regions. Unlike in ground-state-stable phases, where χ\chi typically decreases to zero from the transition temperature into the ground state, here it maintains a high value over an extended temperature range, as shown in Fig. 3. This persistent response indicates enhanced magnetic fluctuations due to free spins that change configuration between two adjacent stable phases.

D. Magnetic Structure and Thermodynamic Stability of EE Phases

To further understand the magnetic structure, stability, and disorderness of EE phases EEI–II\text{EE}_{\text{I--II}} and EEII–III\text{EE}_{\text{II--III}}, we studied the behavior of the magnetic order parameter MM and normalized entropy S/S∞S/S_{\infty} within narrow intervals of the local static field near the phase boundaries. At PB I-II with Hloc/Jeff=2H_{\text{loc}}/J_{\text{eff}}=2, the magnetic order parameter MM rises and saturates at 0.46 at the ground state, indicating that rI∼54%r_{\text{I}}\sim 54\% of tetrahedra are 2I2O and rII∼46%r_{\text{II}}\sim 46\% of tetrahedra are 3I1O/1I3O. The spin structure and tetrahedral distribution are sketched in Fig. 4 (left panel). The positive and negative magnetic charged tetrahedra are located in alternating layers. We have performed Fourier transformation and did not observe any other ordering of these tetrahedra. Indeed, the ground state entropy of this EE state is as high as S≈0.69​S∞≈12​kB​ln⁡(2.6)S\approx 0.69S_{\infty}\approx\frac{1}{2}k_{\text{B}}\ln(2.6) per spin as shown in Fig. 4 (left panel), consistent with the absence of magnetic order. Close to the ground state, even small shifts in Hloc/JeffH_{\text{loc}}/J_{\text{eff}} result in sharp changes in MM and S/S∞S/S_{\infty}, reflecting a high sensitivity to the local static field as shown in Figs. 4 and 4 (left panel) respectively. However, as temperature increases to kB​T/Jeffk_{\text{B}}T/J_{\text{eff}} = 0.71 (T∼1​KT\sim 1\,\text{K}), the system converges toward a common thermodynamic behavior with well-defined MM and S/S∞S/S_{\infty}. These behaviors indicate that the EEI–II\text{EE}_{\text{I--II}} phase is highly disordered and not stable at the ground state but stable at elevated temperatures. The step-like behavior of the order parameter is consistent with previous Monte Carlo simulation results [26], and, together with the corresponding step-like behavior in entropy, provides evidence for the existence of the EE phase. The EEII–III\text{EE}_{\text{II--III}} phase exhibits a magnetic order parameter MM of 1.36, and a ground state entropy of S≈0.48​S∞≈12​kB​ln⁡(1.94)S\approx 0.48S_{\infty}\approx\frac{1}{2}k_{\text{B}}\ln(1.94) per spin. The magnetic structure should have rII∼64%r_{\text{II}}\sim 64\% percent of 3I1O/1I3O tetrahedra and rIII∼36%r_{\text{III}}\sim 36\% of AIAO tetrahedra indicated in Fig. 4 (right panel). Similar thermodynamic behavior is observed around the EEII–III\text{EE}_{\text{II--III}} phase as shown in Figs. 4 and 4 (right panel). We compute the uncertainties for the order parameter MM and normalized entropy S/S∞S/S_{\infty}, which are very small, typically of order 10−410^{-4} and 5×10−45\times 10^{-4}, respectively (see Note 3 of Supplemental Material [32] see also Ref. [33] therein for a detailed error analysis).

The EE phase tetrahedra fractions and entropy can be understood by entropy maximization. Take EEI-II{}_{\text{I-II}} phase for example, the entropy can be naively viewed as a combination of the phase I (2I2O) configurational entropy sI=0.5​kB​ln⁡(1.5)s_{\text{I}}=0.5k_{\text{B}}\ln(1.5) and the phase II (3I1O) configurational entropy sII=0.5​kB​ln⁡(1.3)s_{\text{II}}=0.5k_{\text{B}}\ln(1.3), weighted by their respective volume fractions rIr_{\text{I}} and 1−rI1-r_{\text{I}}, together with an additional entropy term from the random mixing of tetrahedra. Accordingly, the entropy per spin can be expressed as

SI-II=rI​sI+(1−rI)​sII+0.5​kB​[−rI​ln⁡rI−(1−rI)​ln⁡(1−rI)].S_{\text{I-II}}=r_{\text{I}}s_{\text{I}}+(1-r_{\text{I}})s_{\text{II}}+0.5k_{\text{B}}\big[-r_{\text{I}}\ln r_{\text{I}}-(1-r_{\text{I}})\ln(1-r_{\text{I}})\big].

At the phase I–II boundary, where both phases are energetically degenerate, the volume fraction ratio is determined by maximizing SI-IIS_{\text{I-II}}. Solving d​SI-II/d​rI=0\text{d}S_{\text{I-II}}/\text{d}r_{\text{I}}=0 yields rI=53.6%r_{\text{I}}=53.6\%, rII=46.4%r_{\text{II}}=46.4\%, and SI-II=74.0%​S∞S_{\text{I-II}}=74.0\%S_{\infty}. Similarly, applying the same entropy model to the EEII-III{}_{\text{II-III}} phase gives rII=56.5%r_{\text{II}}=56.5\%, rIII=43.5%r_{\text{III}}=43.5\%, and SII-III=60.0%​S∞S_{\text{II-III}}=60.0\%S_{\infty}. Compared to the Monte Carlo simulation results in Fig. 4, these estimates are qualitatively consistent but show some quantitative discrepancies. Such discrepancies arise because this simplified entropy model does not account for additional geometric constraints that emerge when different types of tetrahedra coexist and share common spins, causing their configurational entropy contributions to deviate from the bulk values.

E. Entropic origin of EE phases

To understand the thermodynamic origin of EE phases, we analyze the energy, entropy, and free energy landscape of the system. These phases cannot be stabilized by minimization of internal energy alone, but emerge at finite temperatures due to the competition between internal energy and entropy, governed by the free energy expression F=U−T​SF=U-TS. We begin by examining the energy landscape at zero temperature. Figure 5 shows the internal energy UU as a function of Hloc/JeffH_{\text{loc}}/J_{\text{eff}} for the three stable phases, 2I2O (I), 3I1O/1I3O (II), and AIAO (III), as well as the two EE phases, EEI–II\text{EE}_{\text{I--II}} and EEII–III\text{EE}_{\text{II--III}}. At kB​T/Jeff=0k_{\text{B}}T/J_{\text{eff}}=0, the system favors the configuration with the lowest energy: Phase I dominates for Hloc/Jeff<2H_{\text{loc}}/J_{\text{eff}}<2, Phase II for 2<Hloc/Jeff<62<H_{\text{loc}}/J_{\text{eff}}<6, and Phase III for Hloc/Jeff>6H_{\text{loc}}/J_{\text{eff}}>6. The EE phases, while higher in energy, are close in magnitude near the phase boundaries, suggesting the possibility of competition once entropy is considered. To probe this entropic stabilization, we evaluate the free energy F=U−T​SF=U-TS at kB​T/Jeff=0.21k_{\text{B}}T/J_{\text{eff}}=0.21 (TT = 0.3 K), as shown in Fig. 5. At this elevated temperature, EE phases now attain the lowest free energy in narrow windows near the respective phase boundaries, demonstrating that these phases are stabilized by entropy. To further test this picture, we estimate the boundaries of the EE regions by applying the free energy equilibrium condition

Δ​F=Δ​U−T​Δ​S=0\Delta F=\Delta U-T\Delta S=0 (4)

The resulting contours from Eq. 4 are plotted as solid lines in Fig. 5 and compared to the actual simulated phase boundaries extracted from heat capacity peaks (colored circles). The predicted trends agree qualitatively, capturing the cusp-like shape of the boundary near both EE phases, though the estimated crossover temperature is slightly higher than that observed in simulation. This discrepancy can be attributed to two simplifying assumptions in our analysis. First, the boundary estimation uses ground-state values of UU and SS, neglecting their temperature dependence. Second, the heat capacity peaks reflect a characteristic crossover temperature in the simulation, whereas our analysis implicitly assumes a sharp first-order transition. In reality, the transitions into EE phases are gradual and fluctuation-driven, not symmetry-breaking. The emergence of EE phases is a direct consequence of entropy-driven free energy minimization in regions of high frustration and near-degenerate energy scales.

Discussion

A promising route to engineer these EE phases is using an external magnetic field. By lifting the degeneracy among spin textures, the magnetic field reshapes the entropy landscape and allows selective tuning of EE phase boundaries. This tunability offers a practical route for field control in magnetic states.

An important extension of this work is to explore the role of quantum fluctuations. Our study has focused on classical pyrochlores with R=R= Dy and Ho, where the large R3+R^{3+} moments behave as Ising spins along the local ⟨111⟩\langle 111\rangle axes. In contrast, for R=R= Er or Yb, the crystal-field ground-state doublets are strongly anisotropic in the XY plane with reduced moments, leading to enhanced quantum fluctuations and tunneling [34, 15]. In such cases, entropy may still play a role in stabilizing intermediate states, but the character of the degeneracy and correlations could be qualitatively different, raising the possibility of distinct thermodynamic signatures and quantum phases.

A natural next step is to investigate how the predicted EE phases can be probed experimentally. Thermodynamic probes such as specific heat and entropy measurements provide direct access to the characteristic entropy plateaus [16], while neutron scattering can resolve the associated spin correlations and dynamics [18, 26]. Magnetic susceptibility would further reveal the field response predicted in this work [16, 18, 26]. To systematically explore the HlocH_{\mathrm{loc}} parameter space, one may employ chemical tuning, such as substituting titanium for iridium, or physical tuning through hydrostatic pressure. While chemical substitution offers a broad tuning range, it inevitably introduces disorder, whereas hydrostatic pressure modifies the lattice environment without adding extrinsic defects. Experimentally, EE states are expected to manifest as double anomalies in specific heat with temperature, together with a decoupling between thermodynamic peaks and magnetic susceptibility features.

The physics of EE phases studied in this work can also be applied to other magnetic systems with frustration and competing interactions, such as quantum spin liquids, artificial spin ice, and quantum spin ice. In these systems, metastability and entropy-driven phenomena may underlie transitions and emergent excitations, opening a gate into the discovery of exotic emergent quantum phases.

More broadly, the ability to stabilize and engineer EE phases has implications that reach beyond magnetism. In condensed matter physics, EE states often act as precursors to exotic phenomena—such as topological phases or non-equilibrium steady states [35, 36, 37, 38]. In materials science, EE states corresponds functionalities in memory devices [39, 40], neuromorphic computing [41, 42, 43, 44], and stochastic information encoding [45, 46].

Conclusion

In this study, we investigated the thermodynamic phase behavior of frustrated pyrochlore magnets R2R_{2}Ir2O7 (R=R= Dy, Ho) using Monte Carlo simulations by tuning the strength of the local static background field Hloc/JeffH_{\text{loc}}/J_{\text{eff}}. Beyond the three known magnetic ground states, frustrated spin ice 2-in–2-out (2I2O) phase, frustrated fragmented 3-in–1-out/1-in–3-out (3I1O/1I3O) phase, and antiferromagnetic all-in–all-out (AIAO) phase, we systematically studied the thermodynamic behavior and physical origin of two enhanced-entropy (EE) phases (EEI-II\text{EE}_{\text{I-II}} and EEII-III\text{EE}_{\text{II-III}}) that appear near the phase boundaries at finite temperatures. These EE states exhibit high magnetic susceptibility, high entropy, and spatially mixed spin configurations of neighboring phases, consistent with enhanced magnetic fluctuations and configurational disorder. Our findings suggest that these states do not result from conventional energetic ordering but are stabilized by entropy through the minimization of free energy in regions of frustrated competition. Unlike typical ordered phases, they remain disordered yet thermodynamically robust across extended temperature and Hloc/JeffH_{\text{loc}}/J_{\text{eff}} ranges. This demonstrates the pivotal role of entropy in governing phase stability in frustrated systems and opens a new avenue for exploring entropic phases in correlated magnets.

Methods

We performed Monte Carlo simulations based on the Ising model on frustrated pyrochlore R2R_{2}Ir2O7 (R=R= Dy, Ho) magnets. These simulations explore accessible spin configurations to determine the thermodynamically probable magnetic states. The model includes nearest-neighbor exchange interactions between the pseudo-Ising moments of the rare-earth ions (R3+R^{3+}), represented as classical binary spins constrained along local ⟨111⟩\langle 111\rangle directions. Simulations were carried out on a 4×4×84\times 4\times 8 pyrochlore lattice with periodic boundary conditions. The spin dynamics were evolved using a hybrid Monte Carlo algorithm that combines single-spin-flip (SSF) Metropolis updates with a worm-loop algorithm (WLA). This hybrid approach ensures ergodicity and enhances phase-space exploration, particularly at low temperatures, preventing the system from becoming trapped in local minima [26].

We use a two-step sampling procedure. The first step is thermal equilibrium, where we perform 2000 cycles of SSF/WLA hybrid updates to allow the system to reach thermal equilibrium. Each cycle includes 1,000 Monte Carlo steps. The convergence of system energy indicating thermal equilibrium are monitored and confirmed (see Supplemental Material note 4 [32]). Following equilibration, we perform 4000 additional cycles. In each cycle there are also 1,000 Monte Carlo steps followed by measurements physical observables including internal energy, monopole density, and other quantities of interest. A total of approximately 1000 temperature steps were carried out. Thermodynamic observables were extracted from the equilibrated spin configurations. The internal energy UU per spin was computed using the nearest-neighbor Ising Hamiltonian, and the specific heat capacity CvC_{v} was calculated from the temperature derivative of energy. The order parameter MM was evaluated using the expression in Eq. 2, and the entropy per spin S⁡(T)S(T) was obtained via Eq. 3. Magnetic susceptibility χ\chi was determined through a linear response method by applying a small static magnetic field B0B_{0} to the system. Specifically, the simulation proceeds in two stages: (1) the system is equilibrated with and without the magnetic field B0B_{0}, and (2) the change in magnetization Δ​m\Delta m due to the application of the magnetic field divided by B0B_{0}. The susceptibility is then computed as χ=Δ​m/B0\chi=\Delta m/B_{0}.

All simulations were implemented in C++. Additional implementation strategies and technical background are discussed in prior work [27, 28].
